summary: Thiamine mononitrate is a stable salt form of vitamin B1 (thiamine) used in dietary supplements and food fortification and to prevent or treat thiamine deficiency states such as beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Thiamine is an essential water-soluble vitamin that, as thiamine pyrophosphate, is a coenzyme in carbohydrate metabolism. It is not an FDA-approved drug in the supplement form (the mononitrate is a recognised dietary-supplement/food-fortification ingredient); for treating significant deficiency, parenteral thiamine hydrochloride is used. This record is based on dietary-reference and pharmacopoeial sources.
indications: Prevention and treatment of thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency
Adjunctive treatment/prevention of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (parenteral thiamine generally preferred for acute disease)

dosage.d: Approx 1.1-1.5 mg daily (recommended dietary allowance range)
dosage.n: Higher amounts in multivitamins are common and safe

dosage.d: 5-30 mg daily, in single or divided doses, until repletion
High-dose IV/IM thiamine (hydrochloride) per protocol; oral mononitrate is inadequate for acute severe deficiency
dosage.n: Give thiamine before glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke

dosage.d: Approx 1.4 mg daily (RDA); supplement as part of antenatal vitamins

admin: Take oral thiamine with or without food
For at-risk patients (alcohol use disorder, malnutrition), give thiamine before or with any glucose load to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Use parenteral thiamine hydrochloride for acute, severe or symptomatic deficiency rather than oral mononitrate
In food fortification, mononitrate is preferred for its stability in dry products
Store tablets in a dry place away from light
moa: Thiamine is converted in the body to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), an essential coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase. These reactions are central to carbohydrate metabolism and the production of ATP and NADPH; deficiency impairs energy metabolism in tissues with high demand (nerves, heart), producing beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to thiamine (rare; chiefly reported with parenteral use)
relative: History of reaction to a previous thiamine injection (use parenteral forms cautiously)

preg: Thiamine is an essential nutrient and is safe at recommended dietary amounts during pregnancy; requirements are slightly increased and it is routinely included in prenatal vitamins.
lact: Safe during breastfeeding and required in breast milk; adequate maternal intake ensures sufficient thiamine for the infant.
renal: Thiamine is generally safe in renal impairment; requirements may increase in patients on dialysis or high-dose diuretics (e.g. furosemide), who can become deficient.
hepatic: Generally safe; thiamine requirements and deficiency risk increase in alcohol-related and other chronic liver disease, where supplementation is often needed.

moderate: Loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) - increase urinary thiamine loss and can contribute to deficiency
minor: Chronic alcohol intake impairs thiamine absorption and utilisation
interactions.food: Alcohol and certain raw foods/tea (containing thiaminases or anti-thiamine factors) can reduce thiamine status; otherwise no important food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use markedly impairs thiamine absorption and storage and is a leading cause of deficiency; supplementation is recommended in alcohol use disorder.
interactions.diagnostics: Generally no interference; whole-blood thiamine or erythrocyte transketolase activity can be measured to assess status if needed.

common: Generally none at oral/dietary doses (very well tolerated)
rare: Local injection-site reactions with parenteral use

monitoring: Clinical improvement of deficiency symptoms (neuropathy, cardiac, cognitive)
No routine laboratory monitoring is generally required for oral supplementation
Observe for hypersensitivity when parenteral thiamine is given
counsel: Vitamin B1 supports your body's use of energy from food
Take it as directed; excess is harmless and passed in the urine as it is water-soluble
If you drink heavily or eat poorly, you may need extra thiamine - discuss this with your clinician
Significant deficiency (numbness, confusion, heart symptoms) needs prompt medical treatment, often by injection
There are no significant side effects at normal doses
pk: Rapidly absorbed orally; metabolic effects as deficiency is corrected
Plasma levels rise within a few hours of an oral dose
Short plasma half-life (~1-2 hours); body stores limited (~2-3 weeks)
Daily intake needed; excess is excreted in urine
Store in a dry place at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Not an FDA-approved drug as the mononitrate supplement; it is a recognised dietary-supplement and food-fortification ingredient - this record uses dietary-reference and pharmacopoeial sources
Mononitrate is the stable salt preferred for fortifying dry foods (vs the hygroscopic hydrochloride)
Always give thiamine BEFORE or WITH glucose in at-risk patients to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Oral mononitrate is fine for prevention/mild deficiency, but acute severe deficiency (Wernicke) needs high-dose parenteral thiamine hydrochloride
Water-soluble and very safe; excess is excreted in urine
missed: If a supplement dose is missed, take it when remembered or simply resume the next scheduled dose; do not take a double dose. Consistent daily intake matters more than any single dose.
overdose: Oral overdose is not toxic - thiamine is water-soluble and excess is excreted in the urine. Rare hypersensitivity reactions are associated with rapid intravenous administration; manage any reaction supportively.
